timeline.title: Born a third son
timeline.text: Yi Do was born on 15 May 1397, the third son of Prince Jeongan, who later became King Taejong. As a third son, he was not expected to become king.

timeline.title: Prince Chungnyeong
timeline.text: He was given the title Prince Chungnyeong and married the future Queen Soheon.

timeline.title: A keen student
timeline.text: He was made a Grand Prince and began study with the tutor Yi Su.

timeline.title: Chosen as heir
timeline.text: His elder brother, Crown Prince Yangnyeong, was removed as heir in the sixth month of 1418. King Taejong made the third son the new crown prince.

timeline.title: King at 21
timeline.text: Taejong gave up the throne, and Sejong was crowned on 18 September 1418. His father kept tight control of the army until his own death.

timeline.title: The Tsushima expedition
timeline.text: After famine on Tsushima led to pirate raids on Korea, a fleet of about 227 ships was sent against the island under Taejong's guidance. After 15 days the lord of Tsushima surrendered, and decades of peace and trade with Japan followed.

timeline.title: The Hall of Worthies
timeline.text: Sejong reformed the Hall of Worthies and filled it with gifted scholars, such as Jeong Inji, Sin Sukju and Seong Sammun. It advised the king, taught the royal family and carried out research. Historians have called it a think tank.

timeline.title: Ruling on his own
timeline.text: His father Taejong died in 1422. From then on, Sejong held full power himself.

timeline.title: Time to study
timeline.text: Sejong began a programme that let scholars of the Hall of Worthies research on their own, an idea later compared to modern research grants.

timeline.title: A harsh decree
timeline.text: Not every policy was generous. In 1427 Sejong ordered the small Huihui Muslim community to give up its headwear, close its ceremonial hall and worship like everyone else.

timeline.title: A farming manual
timeline.text: The farming handbook Nongsa jikseol was completed at his order.

timeline.title: Asking the people
timeline.text: Before changing the land tax, the government asked more than 170,000 people for their opinion. The reform took until 1444 to complete.

timeline.title: Instruments for the sky
timeline.text: The engineer Jang Yeong-sil built an armillary sphere turned by a waterwheel, to model the movement of the heavens. The same year, a campaign was sent against Jurchen raiders in the north.

timeline.title: A clock that strikes itself
timeline.text: Jang Yeong-sil completed Korea's first self-striking water clock after studying water clocks in China. The fast new gabin metal printing type was also cast that year.

timeline.title: The northern border
timeline.text: General Kim Jongseo's campaign set up six garrisons and fixed roughly the northern border Korea has today. Sejong also began asking whether smaller tasks could go to the crown prince.

timeline.title: Measuring the rain
timeline.text: On Sejong's order, the royal observatory built an iron rain gauge, the cheugugi, based on an idea of the crown prince, the future King Munjong. From 1442 identical gauges went to every province so rainfall could be compared. Jang Yeong-sil is often credited, but no written record names him.

timeline.title: Jang Yeong-sil's fall
timeline.text: A royal palanquin built by Jang Yeong-sil broke during a journey. He was jailed, flogged and expelled from the palace. Nothing more is known of his life.

timeline.title: Twenty-eight letters
timeline.text: In the twelfth month of 1443, Sejong showed his court a new script of 28 letters. Most scholars think he was closely, personally involved in making it. The basic consonant shapes picture the mouth and tongue as they make each sound.

timeline.title: Officials push back
timeline.text: The scholar-official Choe Malli led a strong protest against the script. Critics argued it turned away from Chinese civilisation; historians add that reading Chinese characters was a mark of high status. Sejong went ahead.

timeline.title: Sharing the load
timeline.text: His health had been getting worse for years. From 1445 the crown prince handled the daily business of government.

timeline.title: The Correct Sounds for the People
timeline.text: In the ninth month of 1446 (about October), the script was proclaimed in the book Hunminjeongeum, The Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People. Sejong wrote its preface. A commentary, the Haerye, was written by scholars led by Jeong Inji.

timeline.title: A dictionary of sounds
timeline.text: The rhyme dictionary Tongguk jeongun was completed.

timeline.title: Death of Sejong
timeline.text: Sejong died on 8 April 1450, at 52, and was buried at Yeongneung. His son became King Munjong.

timeline.title: The script of the state
timeline.text: After centuries in which many officials looked down on it, a decree of November 1894 made Hangul the preferred script for government documents.

timeline.title: The lost commentary found
timeline.text: A copy of the Hunminjeongeum Haerye, the 1446 commentary that explains how the letters were designed, was rediscovered in 1940 after being lost for centuries.

timeline.title: Memory of the World
timeline.text: UNESCO added the Hunminjeongeum Haerye to its Memory of the World register. Koreans mark Hangul Day each 9 October, and Sejong's portrait has been on the 10,000-won note since 1973.

feature.title: The inventions of his reign
feature.lead: Sejong's court made tools for reading, farming and measuring time and weather. Some he made himself; many were built by his scholars and engineers, and each card says who.

items.label: Hangul, the Korean alphabet
items.text: Twenty-eight letters with consonant shapes based on the speech organs. Credited to Sejong himself; most scholars think he was closely involved in the design.

items.label: The Hunminjeongeum and Haerye
items.text: The book that proclaimed the script. Sejong wrote the preface; scholars led by Jeong Inji wrote the commentary explaining the design. Now on UNESCO's Memory of the World register.

items.label: The Hall of Worthies
items.text: A royal research institute of gifted scholars, reformed by Sejong. Its scholars compiled the Hunminjeongeum and other books.

items.label: Research leave for scholars
items.text: A programme letting Hall of Worthies scholars research on their own. Sejong's idea.

items.label: Nongsa jikseol, the farming manual
items.text: An agricultural handbook completed at Sejong's order.

items.label: The great tax survey
items.text: More than 170,000 people were asked their opinion of a land-tax reform before it was carried out.

items.label: Water-driven armillary sphere
items.text: A model of the heavens with rings and an inner globe, turned by a waterwheel. Built by Jang Yeong-sil.

items.label: Gabin metal type
items.text: A new set of cast metal printing type, said to print about twice as fast as before. Credited to Jang Yeong-sil.

items.label: The self-striking water clock
items.text: Korea's first water clock that announced the hours by itself. Built by Jang Yeong-sil, a former government slave whom Sejong gave a post at court.

items.label: Cheugugi, the rain gauge
items.text: An iron cylinder for measuring rainfall, built by the royal observatory on the crown prince's idea. Identical gauges in each province let rainfall be compared across the country.

items.label: Supyo, the water gauge
items.text: A gauge for measuring the height of river water. Credited to Jang Yeong-sil.

items.label: Chiljeongsan, the astronomical calendar
items.text: An astronomical calendar compiled by the court's astronomers, including Jang Yeong-sil.

items.label: Tongguk jeongun, the rhyme dictionary
items.text: A rhyme dictionary completed late in his reign.

works.title: Hunminjeongeum (The Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People)
works.text: The book that proclaimed the new 28-letter script, with Sejong's own short preface explaining why he made it.

works.title: Hangul
works.text: A phonetic alphabet whose basic consonants picture the speech organs. Today it is counted as 24 basic letters in South Korea.

works.title: The Hall of Worthies
works.text: A royal research institute that gathered and supported gifted scholars until 1456.

works.title: Nongsa jikseol
works.text: An agricultural treatise completed at his order.

works.title: Land-tax reform and public survey
works.text: A tax reform prepared by asking more than 170,000 people for their views, completed in 1444.

works.title: The self-striking water clock
works.text: Built by Jang Yeong-sil under Sejong's patronage.

works.title: Gabin metal type
works.text: Faster cast metal type for printing books.

works.title: Cheugugi rain gauges
works.text: Standard rain gauges sent to every province from 1442, so rainfall could be recorded the same way everywhere.

works.title: Chiljeongsan astronomical calendar
works.text: A calendar of the heavens compiled by court astronomers.
